newsitem.title: CYPRUS: FEATURE-Economist assesses impact of Cyprus federation.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Economist assesses impact of Cyprus federation.

text.p: Cyprus has been described as one of the toughest nuts to crack in world affairs, a flashpoint for a potential war between Greece and Turkey and a major factor affecting stability in the eastern Mediterranean.
It is also a case study for economists who, if a settlement is ever thrashed out, will face the arduous task of bringing together two economies that could not be more different.

Divided by a Turkish invasion in 1974 sparked by a brief Greek Cypriot coup engineered by the military government then ruling Greece, Greek Cypriots remain huddled in the south of the island and Turkish Cypriots in the north.

In the internationally recognised Republic of Cyprus, Greek Cypriots -- 40 percent of them made refugees in 1974 -- now have a thriving economy based on services, tourism and offshore business. Inflation has not exceeded 6.5 percent in years.

Across barbed wire, Turkish Cypriots live with double-digit inflation, languish under a European Union trade embargo and are shunned by the international community, which refuses to recognise their breakaway state declared in 1983.
Now, Greek Cypriot economist Andreas Theofanous has given politicians something to mull over in his book "The Political Economy of a Federated Cyprus".

It is a topic politicians on both sides have steered clear of for more than 22 years, but the book provides an insight into the workings of economic convergence in a federation, the accepted basis for a solution to the Cyprus problem under agreements signed by the two sides in 1977 and 1979.
In his book, a sequel to a 1994 edition in Greek, Theofanous examines the impact of two types of federation -- a loose system and a strong one.

The two models vary, but Theofanous argues that in both cases vital issues such as foreign trade and banking should be handled by the central government. He proposes a single central bank and one currency.

United Nations-sponsored talks on reuniting the island as a bi-communal, bizonal federation have been sputtering on for years. One of the points of dispute is how strong, or loose, a federation will be.

"I think the reality lies somewhere in between," said Theofanous, a former economic adviser to ex-president George Vassiliou and now director of the research and development centre at Intercollege, a private college in Nicosia.
Theofanous acknowledges that neither community will get exactly what it wants, implying that both sides will have to yield a little to meet half way if a settlement is to be found.
"In both cases there needs to be the will to make it work," he told Reuters.
Greek Cypriots, the vast majority of whom consider acceptance of a federation the ultimate concession, favour a settlement with a strong central government.

In contrast, he argues, Turkish Cypriots officially favour a model closer to a confederation, with freedom of movement, settlement and the right to own property curtailed with each of two separate areas inhabited by a single ethnic group -- similar to the situation existing today.
Theofanous argues that a loose federation, while impeding economic convergence, is the safest and most efficient option of the two, at least in the initial stages.

"A strong federation is likely to entail more sources of friction," he said. "On the contrary, in a loose federation where most of the powers would belong to the states or cantons, the sources of friction would be minimised."
It would also cost less than a strong federation and function better, Theofanous argues.
This option would satisfy the demand of Greek Cypriots for functionality, and Turkish Cypriots' demand for prosperity, which the current situation does not provide.
Theofanous said the loose federal system would also help Turkish Cypriots retain their identity and allow them to be members of the European Union with Greek Cypriots.

Territorial adjustments in favour of Greek Cypriots are an integral part of the solution. Turkish troops occupy 37 percent of Cyprus's territory. Theofanous suggests the Turkish Cypriot canton retain 25 percent.
"Whatever is signed will be, from a constitutional point of view, a deterioration of the existing conditions for the Greek Cypriots," said Theofanous.
"There should be substantial territorial concessions in exchange for a new constitution which will legalise a set of new arrangements that benefit the Turkish Cypriots."

It would be ideal, he said, to arrive at a solution without going through stages. But if that proves impossible, the second best approach would be a package of measures addressing basic issues and including practical steps to improve the situation.

Theofanous suggests a freeze on Greek Cypriot military spending, a pullout of 50 percent of Turkish forces with an explicit timetable for their full withdrawal, and deployment of a multinational peace force.

Transferring the city of Famagusta on the island's southeastern coast to the Cyprus government and facilitating visits of tourists to the Turkish-held areas would also be included in the package of confidence-building measures.

"It is a balanced approach which all the parties involved can accept, provided they take the political decision to resolve the Cyprus problem in a manner which satisfies their minimum, and not their maximum, objectives," said Theofanous.
